rv.q: But 'Billy Elliot' is an exceptional work that exemplifies what the best musicals are all about: collaboration.
"Billy Elliot," the big, smart, London adaptation of the 2000 movie, finally arrived in a production as seriously thrilling as it is deeply lovable.
That “Billy Elliot” is as much an elegy as a celebration is what makes it such a winner.
It celebrates the mineworkers' collective struggle with all the political passion of a Studs Terkel history.
This is a big, brassy, expertly crafted crowd-pleaser that succeeds on multiple levels.
(OK, provinces, cut the snickering.) In London, "Billy Elliot" managed to capitalize on its stirring saga to overcome Elton John's insipid pop-rock score and Lee Hall's clunky book and
If "High School Musical" didn't have the Disney brand plastered all over it, I doubt that very many people would bother to go see it, even in a production as pleasing as this one.
Billy Elliot really does have something for everyone, and that something is, gloriously, art.
But even a few stumbles can't spoil a show that's so sweet and exhilarating that at times you feel like leaping.

Granted, 'Billy Elliot' isn't perfect - a scene with giant dancing dresses might have gone AWOL from some Disney show on ice - but it's still head and toe-shoes above every other show this season. So thanks, Maggie Thatcher, for giving us something to sing about.
On the evidence so far, these young show-stoppers are nailing it.
The characters are drawn in broad strokes, with good humor but little nuance.
The show's a mess, but it's a likable, good-hearted, overstuffed mess; you're more likely to go away feeling puzzled than feeling cheated by its unevenness.
Billy Elliot the Musical is irresistible perfection.
The sequences where Billy learns to dance under the tutelage of Mrs. Wilkinson and her accompanist Mr. Braithwaite are gorgeous.

But if I seem less than completely enthused about what is undoubted the best anti-Margaret Thatcher musical to hit Broadway since Blood Brothers, it's because, despite an interesting story told through exceptionally vivid, dramatic visuals delivered by director Stephen Daldry and choreographer Peter Darling via a mostly excellent cast, the music...
